issues.detail: The Greek 'κακως' (kakōs) means 'badly' or 'ill', but the Vietnamese 'đau nặng' (severely pained/injured) is a specific medical interpretation. More importantly, 'εχων' (echōn) is a participle meaning 'having' or 'possessing'. The Greek structure implies 'a slave who was badly ill,' whereas the Vietnamese 'có một đầy tớ đau nặng' translates to 'had a slave who was severely pained.' While close, the Vietnamese misses the nuance of the state of the slave as the defining characteristic of the possession.

The Greek 'ημελλεν τελευταν' (hemellen teleutan) means 'about to die'. The Vietnamese 'gần chết' (near death) is an acceptable rendering, but the Greek 'ημελλεν' specifically denotes an imminent state.
